if your plan always falls apart around week five, that's not you failing. that's the part everyone hits.

the results run behind the work. for a stretch you do everything right and the mirror says nothing back. that's the valley, and it's exactly where most men quit.

count the streak, not the mirror. if you're still showing up at week six it starts to show.

week five isn't proof it doesn't work. it's the test.

most men blame the hormone before they check the habits.

5 signs it was never your testosterone:

1. you wake up already tired and that is a sleep quality problem, not a hormone one 2. you dread starting, not the actual work, that is dopamine not drive 3. you cannot begin anything without coffee so the caffeine is running your mornings 4. you crash hard at 3pm which is what a big rushed lunch does to anyone 5. eight hours in bed still feels like six because of late screens and no wind down

fix the inputs for six weeks before you pay for a test.

a friend told me the other night that there are no loyal women left in this generation. i asked him one thing. are you being the man a loyal woman would actually want. he went quiet. most guys do. it is easier to say the problem is out there than to look at what you are building.

being a real man was never about testosterone or a hundred pushups a day. it is having the discipline to actually run your life and still being able to have fun like a kid. and when something around you needs protecting, you stand up. that is it. the angry guy with the ego was never the strong one, that is just what netflix sold you.

women are not the problem. you are what you consume. your beliefs, your environment, your habits, the people you spend your time with. work on that first and the right person tends to show up on her own. skip it and you keep meeting the same woman with a different face.

you can pull up in a lamborghini and still not keep a loyal woman. notice i never mentioned money once. money gives you stability, not the right partner. if you have the money and the ego you attract people who are comfortable around ego, and then you act surprised when they treat you the way you treat everyone else.

short relationships, same ending, every time. before you blame her look at the circle you keep walking back into. maybe it takes a year, maybe ten, who knows. but do not reach for the easy excuse that there are no loyal women left. that one is just you lying to yourself.

Being big stopped being the flex a long time ago.

Half the physiques you're comparing yourself to are held together by a needle and a photo timer. That's not the standard. It never was.

If you added 15 kilos and lost your pull up, you didn't get stronger. You got heavier. Mass you can't use is just decoration.

A client of mine picked calisthenics over the gym for one reason. Not aesthetics, not size. He said it himself: you are in control of your body.

That's the only number worth chasing.

comment "mentality" for the guide

It's not your blood work. It's your week.

The phone you reach for before your feet even hit the floor. No hormone does that.

The gym you dread while you find three hours for everything else. That's not low drive. That's priority, and priority is a decision.

The Monday you spend recovering from a weekend that wasn't even that good. I stopped drinking at 19 and Mondays stopped being a debt I had to pay.

The restart you've done more times than the start. Every time you blamed something new. It was never any of that.

You keep closing the window before anything gets the chance to grow.

comment "mentality" for the guide

Big used to mean discipline. Now it just means one thing he optimized.

The look people actually want isn't bigger anymore. It's clean, defined, moves well, still fits his clothes. Somebody who looks like he could go for a run or climb something.

The number that actually matters isn't on the scale. It's what you can do per kilo you carry. If you added mass and lost your pull up, you didn't get stronger. You got heavier.

Big and stiff is just another way to be out of shape.

I had the body and the business. And I still fell flat.

Nothing changed in my blood. What changed is I stopped doing the small things.

At 19 I trained alone in a garage because it was the only hour of the day nobody had an opinion about me. No money, no coach, no supplements. I didn't stop because none of that ever built anything.

Years later I had everything I was missing back then, and I still hit a wall. Turns out the wall was never about resources. It was about the small things I quietly stopped doing once I had enough of an excuse not to.

You don't outgrow the basics. You just find better excuses to skip them.

I started at 49 kilos and got laughed at for it.

For years the only thing in my head was get bigger, get bigger, get bigger, and I did. I put on size and got strong.

But the thing that ever actually made people look twice was never the size, it was a good move. A clean muscle up gets more attention than someone who's just big, every single time.

I spent years chasing the wrong number before I figured that out.

One of my clients unlocked a front lever, 70kg weighted dips, and 15kg weighted muscle-ups in under a year.

Everyone assumes that means he trained harder than everyone else, but he didn't.

Before he came to me he was doing what most people do: copying workouts off Instagram, guessing at progressions, comparing himself to guys years ahead of him. Guessing wastes time, it's the fastest way to stay stuck.

Here's what actually changed things:

1. Clarity first
We spent weeks just figuring out where he really was, no program no progressions, just understanding his starting point.

2. Load over volume
Once his form was solid we added small amounts of weight early instead of chasing more sets. Low load, better execution and faster progress.

3. Recovery got the same respect as training
Sleep, sunlight, tracking his deep sleep, not an afterthought anymore.

None of this is complicated, it's just consistent and specific to him.

comment "method" and I'll walk you through the rest of it.

We spend almost our entire life sleeping. Most guys still treat it like an afterthought.

With one of my clients, we gave recovery the exact same priority as training, not "sleep more," actual specifics:

1. Mouth tape
Keeps you breathing through your nose all night. Sounds small. Changes everything about sleep quality.

2. Magnetic nasal dilators
Better than the adhesive strips, opens the airway without the residue.

3. Track your deep sleep, not just hours
If your deep sleep is under 40 minutes, you're not actually resting, no matter how long you were in bed.

4. Morning sunlight
Non-negotiable. Same priority as the first set of the day.

You can't out-train bad recovery. If you're not treating sleep like part of the program, you're missing a ton of progress you already earned in the gym.

Belief doesn't always start with you.

One of my clients asked me, half-joking, if I actually thought he'd ever hit 70kg on weighted dips. He didn't believe it yet.

I did. Not because I'm an optimist, because I'd been checking his numbers every single week, and the evidence was already there before he could see it.

That's most of what the beginning of coaching actually is. Someone holding the belief you haven't earned the right to feel yet, based on facts instead of feelings, until you catch up to what's already true about you.

You don't need to believe in yourself today. You need someone who's actually watching the work closely enough to believe it for you.
